confounds: The label distribution is highly imbalanced: 619 diagnosed versus 5,463 controls, so raw accuracy and keyword counts are prior-sensitive.
Diagnosed users are more prolific on average; raw post frequency overweights them, while controls contribute many more total posts and can dominate pooled counts.
Timeline retention and collection windows may differ across accounts; source order does not establish clinical duration or persistence in calendar time.
Age, gender, socioeconomic status, region, occupation, student status, and online-community membership are unobserved and may drive both language and labels.
Labels may reflect self-disclosure, keyword-based sampling, annotation policy, or other collection artifacts rather than confirmed clinical status.
Therapy, psychology, psychiatry, medication, diagnosis, and mental-health terms can refer to another person, professional/academic content, advocacy, or a different condition.
Controls are not guaranteed to be psychologically healthy; genuine distress, self-labeling, or false negatives are plausible.
Bereavement, physical illness, exams, work stress, relationship conflict, and temporary crises can mimic depressive language without a persistent syndrome.

caveats: Retention-window length and posting behavior may differ by source or demographic group.
Higher volume can inflate apparent persistence and co-occurrence.
findings.evidence_summary: Volume was higher for diagnosed users in all four folds; median activity was also higher in every fold. This is predictive but not clinically interpretable.
findings.prompt_guidance: Normalize by user, cap per-user evidence, compare activity-matched users, and include timeline length only as a nuisance feature.

quantitative_support.effect: Diagnosed users averaged about 620 posts versus 530.5 for controls.
Higher in every development fold.

findings.signal: Diagnosed users are modestly more prolific, making raw post counts and repeated opportunities for keyword hits a major confound.

caveats: The first-person and exclusion rules are heuristic, not semantic.
Some diagnosed users have no such posts, so absence is not a strong negative.
findings.evidence_summary: The user-level gap remained positive in every fold, and persistence across separated timeline segments strengthened the separation.
findings.prompt_guidance: Prefer repeated, self-directed, non-quoted mental-health content across the timeline; require corroborating context rather than one keyword.

quantitative_support.effect: +24.6 percentage points; 1.9x raw post rate.

findings.signal: Repeated, agent-centered mental-health language is more useful than isolated symptom words.

caveats: Therapy and psychology are common in controls and can reflect education, work, advocacy, or helping someone else.
Diagnosis and clinical terms may refer to ADHD, autism, physical illness, or humorous pseudo-diagnoses.
findings.evidence_summary: The clinically specific user-level gap was 28.6–35.5% versus 13.2–14.1% across folds; broader care terms showed the same direction.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use care language only when it is first-person, non-quoted, and linked to persistent personal experience; separate depression from other diagnoses and professional discussion.

quantitative_support.effect: 2.4x user prevalence and about 2.3x post rate.

findings.signal: Clinical-care and psychiatric-specific language is a stable association, but it is vulnerable to explicit-diagnosis leakage and role/topic confounds.

caveats: Counts are sparse and include indirect or fictional references.
Do not infer current intent, severity, or causality from lexical presence.
findings.evidence_summary: The direction was stable, but many hits can be third-person, media-related, joking, or supportive discussion rather than self-report.
findings.prompt_guidance: Require self-directed grammatical agency and non-quoted context; treat as a high-sensitivity cue requiring corroboration, not as a diagnosis or risk judgment.

quantitative_support.effect: About 1.9x user prevalence and 1.9x post rate.
Positive in every fold, ranging from 13.5–20.0% versus 7.5–9.4%.

findings.signal: Self-harm and suicide-related vocabulary is relatively more concentrated among diagnosed users but remains rare and highly context-sensitive.

caveats: The broad word family conflates clinical anxiety with excitement and everyday stress.
User-level prevalence is sensitive to one-off mentions.
findings.evidence_summary: Many uses describe anticipation, exams, events, waiting, or ordinary nervousness; normalized post rates were effectively equal.
findings.prompt_guidance: Prioritize persistent, self-described impairment or care-seeking over anticipatory or situational anxiety expressions.

quantitative_support.effect: +14.8 percentage points at user level, but virtually no post-rate difference.
User-level direction was positive in all folds.

findings.signal: Anxiety language separates users more than posts, indicating activity and semantic ambiguity.

caveats: These terms are compatible with temporary stress, work, exams, illness, and humor.
High prevalence implies many false positives even with a stable group difference.
findings.evidence_summary: The user-level direction was stable, yet these cues occur in most users and are easily inflated by posting volume and ordinary life complaints.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use counts, concentration, persistence, and co-occurrence with direct clinical context; downweight mere presence of sadness, tiredness, crying, or sleep words.

Small-to-moderate user-level gap; raw post rate modestly higher.

findings.signal: Generic negative affect, fatigue, and sleep terms are slightly more prevalent among diagnosed users but have poor specificity.

caveats: The detector is intentionally broad and can include non-clinical word forms.

findings.evidence_summary: Controls frequently use the term in colloquial, media, fandom, financial, or humorous contexts; diagnosed users also use it in quoted or public-discussion contexts.
findings.prompt_guidance: Do not score the keyword alone. Require first-person agency, non-quotation, non-media context, and persistence; guard against Portuguese morphological false matches.

User-level direction held in all folds.

findings.signal: A depression-related string is attractive at user level but weak at post level and contaminated by lexical and contextual ambiguity.

caveats: The context audit uses heuristic markers and is not a gold-standard semantic annotation.
Context categories overlap, so percentages should not be summed.
findings.evidence_summary: A pooled post audit showed that only a minority of mental-health hits met the strict clean-first-person heuristic, especially among controls.
findings.prompt_guidance: Add explicit source-type and agency checks; treat quotation marks, named others, media/fiction, memes, irony, and public-health language as counterevidence to personal symptom inference.

quantitative_support.effect: Diagnosed mental-health posts had more first-person cues, but contamination was substantial in both groups.

findings.signal: Mental-health vocabulary is often not autobiographical: quotation, third-person discussion, lyrics/media, jokes, and advocacy are major false-positive mechanisms.

caveats: Controls may include genuine distress or illness despite the control label.
No timestamps were available for a clinical-duration test.
findings.evidence_summary: User-level prevalence was higher for diagnosed users, but raw post rates showed no separation or reversed direction, consistent with activity and collection effects.
findings.prompt_guidance: Look for persistence beyond a situational episode and co-occurring self-directed clinical evidence; use grief, pain, illness, and hospitalization as alternative explanations.

quantitative_support.effect: User prevalence higher in every fold, but raw post rates were equal or control-higher.

findings.signal: Bereavement and physical illness are common, nonspecific sources of distress and should not be treated as depression evidence.

caveats: Topic and community composition may differ by age, interests, and account type.
Humor can coexist with genuine distress, so it is counterevidence to literal interpretation but not proof of absence.
findings.evidence_summary: Controls generated more raw advocacy and joking content because of activity and topic composition, while user-level presence sometimes favored diagnosed users.
findings.prompt_guidance: Downweight public-health education, awareness campaigns, entertainment references, lyrics, memes, irony, and jokes unless supported by direct persistent self-report.

quantitative_support.effect: Higher user prevalence but lower raw post rate for diagnosed users.
Joking markers appeared in about one-tenth of mental-health posts in both groups.

findings.signal: Advocacy, fandom/media discussion, lyrics, and humor can create strong-looking lexical signals without personal symptoms.

negative_results: First-person pronouns alone are non-discriminative: present for 100.0% of diagnosed users and about 99.7% of controls.
A narrow self-reported depression/diagnosis pattern is rare and also occurs in controls; it should not be treated as reliable leakage without context.
Generic anxiety, sleep, crying, fatigue, grief, and physical-illness language is widespread. Several show user-level differences but little or no post-level separation.
Absence of mental-health vocabulary is weak counterevidence: about 15.8% of diagnosed users had no hit from the broad mental-health lexicon.
Medication, therapy, and diagnosis terms can describe ordinary medical care, another person, professional/academic discussion, or jokes; no isolated term was sufficiently specific.
